Pregnancy

Choosing relief for muscle pain in pregnancy

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy can put new demands on your back and other muscles. Before reaching for a warming cream, identify what is in it and check that the treatment fits your stage of pregnancy. There is no single safety rule covering every ointment, gel or patch.

Ask about the exact product

Show a pharmacist, midwife or doctor the package, including its active ingredients and strength. Mention your pregnancy week, where the pain is, how long it has lasted and any other medicines or allergies. A brand name alone may not be enough because different products under that name can have different formulas.

Some rubs contain menthol, camphor or methyl salicylate. Other topical pain medicines contain an anti-inflammatory drug such as diclofenac. These are different treatments, with different precautions. A product available without a prescription still needs a pregnancy check.

Skin is not a complete barrier to medicine absorption. The amount applied, area covered, condition of the skin and use of heat can affect exposure. “For external use” does not mean that there can be no effects elsewhere in the body.

Why pregnancy timing matters

Methyl salicylate, also found in wintergreen oil, requires particular caution. Information about pregnancy exposure is limited. UK teratology guidance considers ordinary use of some muscle rubs unlikely to cause problems, while advising precaution about wintergreen-containing products after twenty weeks. Follow a professional assessment of your actual product rather than treating that as permission for every preparation.

Diclofenac gels carry pregnancy warnings too. NSAIDs can affect fetal kidney function and amniotic fluid from around twenty weeks, with additional fetal circulation concerns later in pregnancy. Do not start an NSAID gel at twenty weeks or later without specific clinician advice; later-pregnancy use may need to be avoided entirely.

Finishing the first trimester does not make all over-the-counter medicines suitable. Likewise, having no aspirin allergy does not establish that a salicylate rub is appropriate. Tell the pharmacist about aspirin sensitivity, and do not substitute concentrated essential oils or homemade mixtures for a checked product.

Separate medicated products from heat treatment

If a professional recommends a topical medicine, follow that product’s directions for amount and duration. Avoid broken or irritated skin and tight coverings unless specifically instructed otherwise. Keep it away from eyes and other sensitive areas, and wash your hands afterwards.

Do not put a heating pad or hot-water bottle over a medicated rub or patch. This combination can cause burns and increase absorption. A strong burning sensation is not a sign that a medicine is working particularly well.

Stop using the product and seek medical advice if you develop significant skin pain, swelling or blisters. Accidental swallowing needs immediate advice from a poison service or urgent medical service.

Build a comfortable daily routine

Try changing position regularly and supporting your back when sitting. A pillow may help you find a comfortable resting position. Stable footwear and avoiding awkward lifting can reduce strain, but pregnancy pain is not a personal failure or proof that your posture is bad.

Gentle movement, such as a comfortable walk, may help. Adjust activities that aggravate symptoms and follow any restrictions given by your maternity team. A physiotherapist can suggest exercises and support for your particular pain rather than a generic routine.

A wrapped cool pack or gentle local warmth may offer short-term comfort when used without a medicated product. Protect your skin and avoid overheating. If you consider massage or acupuncture, discuss it with your maternity team and choose a practitioner experienced in pregnancy; benefit and suitability vary.

When a pain medicine is needed, paracetamol is generally the first choice for mild-to-moderate pain during pregnancy. Check the dose and suitability with a professional and follow the label. Repeated or worsening pain still needs assessment.

For ordinary movement, water-based exercise or gentle stretching may be comfortable alternatives to walking. Choose activity you can tolerate and follow your maternity team’s advice; comfortable low-heeled, supportive footwear can help with balance as your centre of gravity changes.

Know when an ache needs more than a cream

Contact maternity care promptly for significant back pain with fever, painful urination, bleeding, leaking fluid or contractions. Pain under the ribs or new severe pain also deserves assessment. Do not wait weeks or repeatedly cover it up with pain treatment.

Loss of feeling in the legs or genital area, new marked weakness or other severe neurological symptoms need urgent medical attention. A clinician can distinguish a muscular problem from a urinary infection, labour-related pain or another condition.

If you already used a topical product, keep the packaging and ask about the actual exposure. A single application does not automatically mean harm. The useful details are the ingredient, amount, frequency and pregnancy stage.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

FDA warns that NSAIDs from around 20 weeks can affect fetal kidney function and amniotic fluid; topical drug labels and the exact ingredient still need checking.

NHS and BUMPS recommend cause-based assessment, supportive measures and appropriate analgesia for pregnancy pain rather than assuming every warming rub is suitable.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare the label, pregnancy week and symptom details for a pharmacist or maternity clinician. It cannot approve a whole brand or product category.

When to seek help

Never combine a medicated rub or patch with a heat source. Severe pain, fever, urinary symptoms, bleeding, contractions or fluid leakage needs prompt maternity advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check the active ingredient, strength and pregnancy week before using a pain cream.
  • The second and third trimesters have medicine precautions of their own.
  • Never place a heat source over a medicated rub or patch.
  • Seek assessment when pain is severe, persistent or accompanied by other symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Can I apply a warming rub to my pregnant abdomen?

Do not assume this is appropriate. Abdominal pain may need assessment, and the product and application site should be checked with your maternity team.

Is a natural muscle rub safer?

Not necessarily. Essential oils and plant-derived ingredients can be concentrated and may lack adequate pregnancy safety information.

Should I stop prescribed aspirin because a muscle rub contains a salicylate?

No. Prescribed low-dose aspirin for a pregnancy indication is a separate treatment. Ask your maternity clinician before changing it.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
